Lou Gehrig was a first baseman and American League legend best known for his record two thousand one hundred thirty consecutive games played, earning the nickname The Iron Horse. Over seventeen seasons with the Yankees, he was one of baseball's most consistent power hitters and a cornerstone of the franchise's nineteen twenties and nineteen thirties dominance.

Gehrig played two thousand one hundred thirty consecutive games from nineteen twenty-five to nineteen thirty-nine, a record that stood for fifty-six years until Cal Ripken Jr. broke it in nineteen ninety-five. He hit four hundred ninety-three home runs and drove in one thousand nine hundred ninety-five runs; his career three forty batting average ranks among the all-time greats. In nineteen thirty-four, Gehrig won the Triple Crown, leading the league in home runs, RBIs, and batting average—one of the sport's rarest feats.

His career was cut short by amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, now often called Lou Gehrig's Disease. On July fourth, nineteen thirty-nine, he delivered his iconic luckiest man farewell speech to a sold-out Yankee Stadium crowd. He played alongside Babe Ruth during the Yankees' most dominant era, forming one of baseball's greatest duos. Babe Ruth was his predecessor and the other pillar of Yankees dominance in the nineteen twenties and thirties. Joe DiMaggio succeeded him as the Yankees' lead slugger in the following decade. Gehrig spent his entire career with the franchise and became one of its greatest legends.
